Overview

Togo at a Glance

Togo is a French-speaking West African state with a civil law system, membership of OHADA for company and commercial law, and of the West African Economic and Monetary Union (UEMOA), whose regional framework shapes banking and anti-money laundering rules. Companies are recorded in the Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier (RCCM), which according to Togo's extractive industries transparency reporting also holds beneficial ownership information, a requirement introduced through the 2015 Penal Code. Personal data is governed by Law No. 2019-014, and its regulator, the Instance de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (IPDCP), began operating in March 2025. Investigations therefore combine accessible registry material with care over a data protection regime that is still being implemented.

Organisations commission work involving Togo largely because of Lomé's role as a regional gateway. The deep-water port and associated logistics, transit and free zone activity serve landlocked neighbours, and Lomé hosts the headquarters of several pan-African financial groups. Typical requests include due diligence on freight forwarders, traders and transit agents, verification of counterparties in commodity and goods trade, background research on executives and shareholders in banking, telecoms and extractives such as phosphates, and enquiries into trade-based fraud or document irregularities. Investors and lenders also assess politically exposed relationships, given the state's large role in concessions, procurement and port-related businesses.

Law & Regulation

What applies before any work touching Togo begins

Legal system

Togo has a civil law system derived from French law, with codified civil, penal and procedural law and a new Penal Code adopted in 2015. Commercial and company law is set largely by the OHADA Uniform Acts, with the OHADA Common Court of Justice and Arbitration in Abidjan as the final court on uniform law questions. Commercial disputes are heard in the first instance by courts in Lomé, where specialised commercial jurisdiction has been introduced, with appeals to the courts of appeal and the Supreme Court. A Court of Auditors oversees public accounts. Proceedings and filings are in French.

Data protection

Law No. 2019-014 of 29 October 2019 on the protection of personal data · Regulator: Instance de Protection des Données à Caractère Personnel (IPDCP)

Consent is the default lawful basis, with alternatives for legal obligations, public interest tasks, contracts and vital interests; investigative work therefore needs a carefully documented basis. Processing of sensitive data, including ethnic origin, political or religious views, union membership, health, genetic data and sex life, is prohibited subject to exceptions such as legal claims. Transfers to a third country require adequate protection, and the controller must inform the authority before transferring. The IPDCP began its activities in March 2025, initially focusing on awareness and compliance standards, with sanctions to follow. No data localisation requirement has been identified.

Private investigators

We have not identified from the sources reviewed a specific licensing regime for private investigators or detective agencies in Togo, and the position should be confirmed with Togolese counsel before any local enquiry. Surveillance, recording and the collection of personal data are constrained by Law No. 2019-014, the Penal Code and privacy protections, and the processing of sensitive data is prohibited save for limited exceptions. Police, judicial, tax and civil registry records are not available to private parties. TDSC does not seek access to restricted records and coordinates only appropriately qualified local professionals.

Corporate & public records

Companies are registered in the Registre du Commerce et du Crédit Mobilier (RCCM) under OHADA rules, with company formalities typically handled through a one-stop business formalities centre in Lomé. RCCM extracts identify the company, its legal form, registered office and managers. Togo's extractive industries transparency reporting describes the RCCM as also keeping a register of beneficial owners, with declarations required since the 2015 Penal Code; we have not confirmed whether that register is publicly searchable. Extractive sector contracts are subject to disclosure under a 2014 transparency law.

Anti-corruption & AML

Togo's 2015 Penal Code contains corruption offences, and Law No. 2015-006 of 28 July 2015 created the Haute Autorité de Prévention et de Lutte contre la Corruption et les Infractions Assimilées (HAPLUCIA), which can collect information and refer substantiated complaints to the public prosecutor. The Cellule Nationale de Traitement des Informations Financières (CENTIF) is the financial intelligence unit, applying the UEMOA anti-money laundering framework. A 2016 law on access to public information and the Court of Auditors complete the framework.

General information compiled 2026-11-04 from the sources listed below. It is not legal advice; TDSC works with qualified local counsel on questions of law.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters Touching Togo

TDSC scopes Togo engagements from Nashville, starting with a review of what can be lawfully obtained: RCCM extracts, OHADA and official gazette publications, court decisions, transparency reporting and French-language media. Because many matters concern goods and money moving through Lomé to neighbouring countries, we scope research across the relevant UEMOA and ECOWAS jurisdictions rather than Togo alone. Where documents must be retrieved locally or enquiries made, we coordinate appropriately qualified Togolese professionals and work with local counsel. We design data handling around Law No. 2019-014, including its restrictions on sensitive data and its requirement to inform the IPDCP before transfers abroad, and we do not represent that non-public beneficial ownership or government records can be obtained privately.

TDSC has no office in Togo. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope. TDSC does not provide legal advice.

Typical Matters

Where Investigative Work Involving Togo Concentrates

01

Port and logistics counterparties

Verifying freight forwarders, customs brokers, transit operators and warehouse companies linked to the Port of Lomé, including ownership, management, litigation and adverse media, before contracting or extending credit on goods moving to Sahel markets.

02

Trade-based fraud enquiries

Investigating suspected document fraud, misdescribed cargo or phantom shipments in trade routed through Lomé, combining registry checks, shipping and open-source research, and coordinating with local counsel on any steps requiring court involvement.

03

Banking and financial sector backgrounds

Background research on shareholders, directors and senior managers of banks, microfinance institutions and payment businesses operating from Lomé, covering regulatory history, litigation and reputational indicators across the UEMOA region.

04

Extractives and concession diligence

Reviewing partners and contractors in phosphates, clinker and other extractive or concession activities, drawing on RCCM records, transparency reporting under the 2014 law and media sources to assess ownership and political exposure.

05

Agent and distributor screening

Screening commercial agents, distributors and consultants used in Togo and neighbouring markets ahead of appointment, focusing on beneficial ownership, links to public officials and red flags relevant to anti-bribery compliance programmes.

Questions

Togo: Frequently Asked Questions

How do we check a Togolese company?

The core record is an RCCM extract, which under OHADA rules shows legal form, registered office and managers. We cross-check it against official publications, court records and media coverage to confirm the company exists, is active and is run by the people presented. Where records must be obtained in person in Lomé, we coordinate a qualified local professional.

Is beneficial ownership information available in Togo?

Togo requires beneficial ownership declarations, and transparency reporting describes the RCCM as maintaining a beneficial ownership register. We have not confirmed whether it is publicly searchable. We therefore combine registry data, counterparty disclosure supported by documents and open-source research, and identify clearly any ownership questions that remain unresolved.

What does Togo's data protection law mean for our investigation?

Law No. 2019-014 requires a lawful basis, prohibits processing sensitive data except in limited cases such as legal claims, and requires the controller to inform the IPDCP before transferring data abroad. The authority began operating in 2025. We minimise the personal data collected in Togo and document the basis for any transfer to the United States.

Can you look into goods moving through the Port of Lomé?

We can research the companies, individuals and vessels involved using corporate records, shipping data available through lawful sources and open-source material, and identify inconsistencies suggesting fraud. We do not access customs or port authority systems. Where documents held by authorities are needed, local counsel can advise on court or official channels.

Does TDSC have an office in Lomé?

No. TDSC works from Nashville, Tennessee, and has no office, staff or telephone number in Togo. Each engagement is a scoped consulting assignment, and where on-the-ground work is required we coordinate appropriately qualified Togolese professionals and Togolese counsel within the agreed scope.
